paragraphs.title: The Uselessness of the Vine Wood

answers: What it is more than any tree
What color its leaves are
When its fruit will be gathered
easy.explanation: The prophet asks, “what is the vine tree more than any tree?”
easy.q: What does the prophet ask about the vine tree?

answers: A house
A vessel or a pin to hang a vessel on
A forest
easy.explanation: The passage asks whether wood from the vine could be used for any work or as a pin to hang a vessel.
easy.q: What could not be made from the vine wood?

answers: It became stronger
It became a useful tool
The fire devoured both ends and burned the midst
easy.explanation: The fire devoured both ends of it, and the midst of it was burned.
easy.q: What happened to the vine when it was cast into the fire?

answers: The fire weakened and burned it
It became too heavy
It grew too large
medium.explanation: If the whole vine was fit for no work, it is even less fit after the fire has devoured it.
medium.q: Why is the burned vine even less suitable for work?

answers: It becomes a tool and then is burned
It is unfit for work, is burned, and remains unfit for work
It becomes stronger and is used as a pin
medium.explanation: The vine is unfit for work when whole and even less suitable after being burned.
medium.q: Which sequence describes the vine in the passage?

answers: A flowering branch
A clay vessel
A wooden peg for hanging a vessel
medium.explanation: The passage asks whether men would take a pin from the vine to hang any vessel thereon.
medium.q: What does the word “pin” refer to in this passage?

answers: The vine is more useful than the forest trees
The vine is weak and unsuitable as material for work
None of the forest trees can be used for work
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes that the vine is not suitable for making useful objects.
challenge.q: What is the main point of comparing the vine with the trees of the forest?

answers: To show that the fire was not the only reason it was useless
To show that it was suitable for building
To show that the fire did not harm it
challenge.explanation: The vine was already fit for no work before the fire burned it.
challenge.q: Why does the passage mention that the vine was unfit for work when it was whole?

answers: They explain how vines grow
They prove that the vine is useful for every purpose
They emphasize the vine’s lack of usefulness
challenge.explanation: The questions lead to the conclusion that the vine has no real use for making objects, especially after burning.
challenge.q: What effect do the repeated questions about the vine have?

short_answers.question: In verse 5, what is the contrast between the vine when it was whole and after it was burned?
answers: It was fit for some work before but not afterward
It was fit for no work before, and even less fit after being burned
It was stronger after being burned
short_answers.explanation: The verse says the whole vine was fit for no work, and asks how much less useful it would be after the fire.

paragraphs.title: The Parable Applied to Jerusalem’s Inhabitants

answers: A vine tree given to the fire
Strong trees of the forest
A vessel made of metal
easy.explanation: The Lord says He will give the inhabitants of Jerusalem to the fire as a vine tree among the forest trees.
easy.q: To what are the inhabitants of Jerusalem compared?

answers: Water them
Devour them
Turn them into vessels
easy.explanation: The passage says that another fire shall devour them.
easy.q: What will the fire do to them?

answers: He will strengthen them
He will build them a pin
They will face judgment and fire
easy.explanation: Setting His face against them is connected with their going from one fire to another fire that devours them.
easy.q: What will happen when the Lord sets His face against them?

answers: They are described as strong and fit for work
They are compared to green forest trees
They are compared to a vine that is useful only for the fire
medium.explanation: The inhabitants are compared to the useless vine that has been given to the fire for fuel.
medium.q: How is the parable of the vine applied to the inhabitants of Jerusalem?

answers: Leaving one fire does not save them, because another fire will devour them
Leaving the fire brings them safety
Leaving the fire makes them useful vessels
medium.explanation: The verse emphasizes that escaping one fire does not end their danger.
medium.q: What is the relationship between going out from one fire and being devoured by another?

answers: They were born in a forest
They had already experienced severe destruction or judgment
They found material for building
medium.explanation: The image presents them as having come out of one fire while still remaining exposed to another.
medium.q: What does “they shall go out from one fire” suggest in context?

answers: It represents weakness, damage, and uselessness for work
It represents agricultural prosperity
It is stronger than the trees of the forest
challenge.explanation: The burned vine represents something damaged and unfit for useful work, like the judgment described for Jerusalem.
challenge.q: Why is the burned vine an especially fitting picture of Jerusalem’s inhabitants?

answers: They become stronger after the fire
They go out from one fire, but another fire devours them
They become trees of the forest
challenge.explanation: The passage describes escape from one fire followed by destruction from another.
challenge.q: What progression is described for the inhabitants of Jerusalem?

answers: The centrality of judgment and destruction
The beauty of the vine
The possibility of using the vine for building
challenge.explanation: Fire is the dominant image of the judgment coming upon Jerusalem’s inhabitants.
challenge.q: What does the repeated imagery of fire emphasize?

answers: It will become desolate
It will become a forest
It will be filled with vessels
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will make the land desolate.”
easy.q: What will happen to the land?

answers: Because vines grew there
Because its inhabitants committed a trespass
Because the fire went out
easy.explanation: The verse gives their committed trespass as the reason for the land’s desolation.
easy.q: Why will the land become desolate?

answers: The trees of the forest
The inhabitants of Jerusalem
The Lord God
easy.explanation: The verse ends with, “saith the Lord God.”
easy.q: Who speaks the final words of the verse?

answers: Barren, deserted, or laid waste
Fruitful and prosperous
Covered with vessels
medium.explanation: Desolate describes land that is barren, deserted, and ruined.
medium.q: What does the word “desolate” mean in this verse?

answers: The land becomes desolate because its inhabitants committed a trespass
The land becomes fruitful because its inhabitants committed a trespass
The inhabitants committed a trespass because the land became a forest
medium.explanation: Their trespass is the stated cause, and the desolation of the land is the result.
medium.q: What cause-and-effect relationship appears in the verse?

answers: Desolation, then trespass, and finally the Lord’s word
Trespass, then desolation of the land, according to the Lord God
The Lord’s word, then building vessels, and finally desolation
medium.explanation: The verse connects the inhabitants’ trespass with the land’s desolation and identifies it as the word of the Lord God.
medium.q: Which order best summarizes the verse?

answers: It moves from the picture to the result: the land will become desolate
It cancels the imagery of the fire
It teaches that the vine is fit for work
challenge.explanation: After the image of the vine and its application to Jerusalem, the verse gives the result of judgment: desolation.
challenge.q: How does verse 8 conclude the parable of the vine?

answers: The inhabitants acted faithfully
The inhabitants acted treacherously or unfaithfully
The inhabitants made useful vessels
challenge.explanation: A trespass indicates wrongdoing, breach of faith, or treacherous conduct.
challenge.q: What can be understood from the phrase “committed a trespass”?

answers: The desolation is presented as judgment according to the word of the Lord God
The desolation is presented as a mere accident
The desolation is presented as a blessing for the inhabitants
challenge.explanation: The verse presents the desolation as the Lord’s judgment for their trespass.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the land’s desolation and the Lord God’s final statement?

short_answers.question: According to verse 8, what two things are connected by the word “because”?
answers: The land’s desolation and the inhabitants’ trespass
The fire and the making of vessels
The forest trees and the vine’s fruit
short_answers.explanation: The land is made desolate because its inhabitants committed a trespass.

answers: A vine tree
A golden vessel
A cedar house
easy.explanation: The chapter uses the vine tree and its wood as the central illustration.
easy.q: What object is used throughout the chapter as the main illustration?

answers: Usefulness for every kind of work
Weakness and coming judgment
The prosperity of Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The useless and burned vine illustrates the weakness and judgment of Jerusalem’s inhabitants.
easy.q: What does the vine’s condition illustrate?

answers: It becomes desolate
It becomes a forest
It becomes full of tools
easy.explanation: The chapter ends with the Lord declaring that He will make the land desolate.
easy.q: What is the final condition of the land?

answers: Both are described as fit for every work
The inhabitants of Jerusalem are compared to a vine given to the fire
The vine is compared to the strength of Jerusalem’s walls
medium.explanation: The Lord applies the image of the vine given to the fire to Jerusalem’s inhabitants.
medium.q: What is the connection between the useless vine and Jerusalem?

answers: Going out from one fire guarantees safety
Going out from one fire may still be followed by destruction from another
Fire has no effect on the inhabitants
medium.explanation: The inhabitants go out from one fire, yet another fire shall devour them.
medium.q: What does the chapter teach about outward survival from judgment?

answers: The inhabitants committed a trespass
The vine was too fruitful
The forest trees were too strong
medium.explanation: The Lord says He will make the land desolate because they committed a trespass.
medium.q: What reason is given for the land’s desolation?

answers: An object that is useless for its intended purpose cannot claim greater usefulness after destruction
A burned vine becomes stronger than a forest tree
Judgment always produces prosperity
challenge.explanation: The vine is unfit for work when whole and even less useful after being burned, forming the chapter’s central picture.
challenge.q: What central principle does the chapter communicate through the vine image?

answers: They begin with the vine, apply the image to Jerusalem, and end with the land’s desolation
They begin with Jerusalem, then describe a forest, and end with a harvest
They begin with tools, then describe prosperity, and end with peace
challenge.explanation: The passage first describes the vine, then applies it to Jerusalem’s inhabitants, and finally announces desolation.
challenge.q: How do verses 1–8 move from illustration to application?

answers: Trespass leads to the Lord’s judgment and the desolation of the land
Trespass is praised as a sign of faithfulness
Trespass has no effect on the land
challenge.explanation: The final verse directly connects the inhabitants’ trespass with the Lord’s judgment on the land.
challenge.q: What does the chapter show about the relationship between sin and judgment?

short_answers.question: In one sentence, what is the main message of Ezekiel 15?
answers: Jerusalem is compared to a useless vine given to the fire, and its trespass brings desolation
Jerusalem is compared to a strong forest tree that will prosper
The vine is praised as the best material for making vessels
short_answers.explanation: The chapter uses the useless vine as a picture of Jerusalem’s judgment and concludes with the desolation of the land.
